 I journeyed to many locations far and wide,

name: Promise
source_excerpt:
A site specific work inspired by Eliza Emily Donnithorne, a 19 century resident of Camperdown Lodge, corner Georgina Street and King Street, Newtown. 
 Eliza was a social elite and her wedding was to be a gala occasion. The banquet was laid out. Onlookers, coaches and guests assembled to escort Eliza to her wedding at St Stephen’s Church. 
 But the groom never arrived. Eliza retreated to isolation, insisting that her house stay in ready for the arrival of her beloved. The door to the house remained ajar and Eliza could be seen awaiting her fiancés arrival. The wedding table was never cleared and she remained in her wedding dress until she died in 1886. Eliza’s grave is in the graveyard at St Stephen’s Church. 
 It is said that Eliza inspired Charles Dickens to create Miss Havesham in his famous novel, Great Expectations.

We see English houses from Stanmore, London, where the suburbs name derives and Italian migrant ships that transported residents who now live in the neighbourhood. We move on to the present day, with hybrid transport in the medium density suburb, including Parramatta road and the Sydney Rail link. The left side of the mural highlights affordable and accessible housing for people living with disabilities and the importance of building community - the houses being friendly characters, all on the move together.

name: Women’s Honour
source_excerpt:
When asked to paint portraits highlighting notable women from the local area, I was moved to discover the 2019 Women’s Honour Roll. These women were chosen by peers to celebrate empowerment, equality, social justice, and inclusion. 
 I felt portraits had to be vibrant, commanding, and full of life, just as the women were within their communities. Collectively, they are a reminder of the incredible people who work tirelessly and fearlessly to help others in need. The brightly coloured arrangements represent diversity and oneness.
 The women featured in the artwork are: Barbara Spears, advocate for equal pay for women and family working rights; Rosemary Hegner, recognised for her 31 year career with NSW Ambulance; Uppma Virdi - founder of Chai Walli, role model for empowerment and gender parity; and Barbara Ramjan, a long-time champion for the vulnerable from LBGTQIA, people with disabilities, migrants and refugees.

name: Galo and the Cockatoo
source_excerpt: This artwork for Petersham is a juxtaposition of the native Australian cockatoo and the unofficial Portuguese national animal, the rooster. The rooster’s central place in the artwork is designed to reinforce the important connection between the suburb of Petersham and the Portuguese community. It is said that everyone should have a rooster in their home to bring them good luck – now, the luck of the rooster will be brought to all of Petersham. Flying under the same sky, sharing the same space on earth, is the Australian cockatoo. Its place in the artwork reminds us of the Australian way of welcoming all people with open arms to be part of our evolving heritage. The purple tones in the sky reflect the lavender, the Portuguese national flower – a further reference to Australia’s unique cultural melting pot.

name: The Makers
source_excerpt: This artwork pays tribute to the rich artisanal and industrial history of the Camperdown area, in particular, the areas connection to pottery, brick-making and candle-making. In the past, Camperdown was known to house many artisans including potters, brickmakers and candlemakers. The work contains abstract references to several buildings, taken from original drawings of Fowlers Pottery works, pottery vases, pot pants, pipes, brickworks, a candle to represent candle makers, as well as a steam engine, a nod to the rich railway history of the area. The fence next to the wall itself is made from retired local railway sleepers, preserving the local railway memory.

name: A Rising Tide
source_excerpt:
In one of Newtown’s iconic terrace houses, a young student sits; she reacts in alarm to an impending flood that surges into her life. The youth depicted is struggling with a housing and rental crisis, where life means keeping her head above water. As the tide rushes in, she knocks over the vase of flowers, asking us to question how our actions may impact nature, even if they are involuntary.
 The rising tide represents the issues felt by the new generation and addresses the impact past human decisions have made on the local environment, resulting in pollution, flooding and the dwindling of native sea life. This artwork stands as a monument to concern and action against the problems that this new generation faces.

The artwork highlights the talents of refugees and their contributions to the diversity, vitality and inclusiveness for which the Inner West is renowned and loved.
  Young artists, Raneen Shamon and Emmanuel Asante were mentored and assisted Fintan to create the work.

name: Silvereye

 Jacquie mentioned that the garden that runs along the side of her house (where the artwork is situated), was built due to her gathering the leaf litter from these Callistermon Salignus trees (across the road), to create the mulch for this garden. This is the reason I wanted to incorporate the Callistermon Salignus flowers.

name: Rivers Flow
source_excerpt:
Commissioned for the River Canoe Club, the collaborative design by artists Zachary Bennett-Brook a contemporary Indigenous artist of Torres Strait Islander ancestry, born and raised in Dharawal Country (Wollongong), and Kim Siew a local female artist, embraces the surrounding area of the Cooks River, playing with the theme of water and the reflections of the natural environment.
 The artwork mimics the movement of water, wrapping around the building in a smooth flowing manner, incorporating Zac's Indigenous styled patterns which represent water and meeting places. Kim's work links in, with silhouettes of local mullet fish and water birds, as well as plants which are found along the river's edge. People in canoes and kayaks paddle throughout the artwork, a nod to River Canoe Club, NSW's oldest canoe club - a place where canoes and kayaks used to be crafted from wood by hand.
 Blue tones flow through the work, representing both the water and sky, with different viewing points added, a view from above, and a view from a canoe, or from across the water.

Specifically the amazing team responsible for the rejuvenation of the Cooks River aside the Marrickville Golf Course. It’s works like these that encourage species like the Sacred Kingfisher to return to our urban environments.

name: Shared Ground
source_excerpt:
This welcoming part of country is where Gadigal and Wangal people have lived, it was & always will be Aboriginal land. Petersham Park may once have been good kangaroo ground. Today the park has a mix of native and introduced flora and fauna, some nocturnal, which locals enjoy & we celebrate here. 
 Petersham Oval has been a place to gather and play games for many generations. 
 In 1936 fast bowler Mollie Flaherty practiced her graceful style on the ovals of the Inner West. She played for NSW and was in the first Australian women's team to tour England in 1937. Mural painted with gratitude to this ground we share.

name: Caroline Chrisholm Behind Glass
source_excerpt:
This portrait celebrates Caroline Chisholm (1808-1877), a social reformer known 
 for her support for young female immigrants and family welfare. 
 Forming part of a series of paintings titled Lost Figures the work acts as a depiction of forgotten or obscure historical figures in Australian history. Painted in a frosted or beveled glass effect the obscured figures are presented as abstract, forgotten, or distant. 
 The work aims to create dialogue around how history is written and recognised in our communities, to provide an alternative to how historical figures are represented in public art, exploring Australia's relationship with underdog figures and challenging notions of who should be allowed representation. 
 Interesting note: Caroline Chisholm was in regular contact with Charles Dickens, her stories of Sydney inspired a number of important characters in Dickens Novels. In Dickons' novel Bleak House the character of Mrs Jellyby is said to be an amalgamation of three women of the period, including Caroline Chisholm.

 The sense of colour and playfulness and expressing oneself though fashion is evident when walking the streets of Newtown and Enmore. Here the prints of bright candy colours of the old-fashioned sweets adorn the clothing of locals. 
 The dog to the left, is a nod to Nugget a well-known and much-loved local character. 
 Candy represented on the clothing prints: Humbugs, Jubes, Sherbet, Freckles, Fried Eggs.

name: Animal Wall - Salmon Playground
source_excerpt:
I enjoy patterns. I love looking at them, and for them. It’s said that humans are pattern seeking creatures - it’s how we find meaning. I don’t know if that’s true, but I find meaning in pattern creation. There is something deeply satisfying about finding a way of making complex and disparate objects and themes work together.
 
 This work draws on animal creatures of the Inner West and Salmon Playground for inspiration; featured are dogs, cats, possums, rats, ibis, bats, pigeons, skinks, minors, lorikeets and Australian raven. It’s a pleasure to think that this park is as useful to all these and more critters as it is for us - everyone fitting together - nice pattern.

name: Goolay'yari
source_excerpt:
Cooks River has another name, Goolay'yari. First Nations peoples were nurtured by the pristine Goolay'yari, through fishing, birding and feasting upon the once abundant plant life and shellfish. Auntie Fran Bodkin tells the dreaming story of the Pelican man, Goolay'yari. 
 The 'Goolay'yari' artwork is a night-time scene which celebrates the local flora and fauna of 'Cooks River' and the surrounding Gumbramorra wetlands that feed into the 
 river. It depicts edible saltbushes, native grasses, godwits, Garal'ga (yellowtail black cockatoo), Muruduwin (fairy wren) 
 and a large Goolay'yari/Garranga bumarri (pelican). 
 David Cragg is an artist of Irish, Scottish, Bundjalung and Biripi ancestry, working in Dharawal Country, but who grew up on local Wangal, Gadigal and Bidjigal Country. 
 David sees this artwork as a way of giving back to the lands that raised him and the vibrant communities that call the area home. This work was developed in consultation with the CHOICE team as well as Council’s Aboriginal Programs and Urban Ecology teams. David Cragg conducted immense research in the development of this work to discover the stories surrounding the Gumbramorra Swamp of Cooks River, sitting between Marrickville and Sydenham, much of which has now been drained and developed upon.

name: Give and Take

I really love to respond with imagery that is derived 
 from the local community. The images start with taking photographs, giving me a chance to build a personal relationship with the people of the area. 
 This building houses a local gym. Themes central to the gym, pushing past mental and physical barriers, as well as working hard, is reflected here in the artwork. 
 The background colours are vibrant and eye-catching, juxtaposed against the realistic and extremely rendered out depictions of local gym individuals. This artwork is a celebration of this dynamic community. The lady featured is a gym instructor and local community member.

I love to bring out the human aspect of my subjects in giant scale street art portraiture. 
 The expression and loose brush strokes celebrate the past, the present and future, and the impermanent nature of all things. It is champions of the past that create our future. 
 Renowned for its motorbike collections and innovation, for nearly 50 years Procycles has been deeply involved in grass roots motorcycle sport and communities - mentoring young riders from dirt riding to the tar, sponsoring Australian champions, such as 70's motorcycle legends - Warren Willing, Gregg Hansford and Ken Blake - celebrated here.

Framed by the aesthetics of a Greek pottery style and the green and gold colour scheme of classic Australiana, the mural explores and pays tribute to the Greek-Australian community in modern day Marrickville, 200 years after the Greek War of Independence.
 Hestia, goddess of the home and hearth is depicted leaving her throne in Olympus to settle here in Marrickville where she lights her hearth fire anew for the families of the migrant community.

name: Birds of Lewisham

 The Red Wattlebird, Superb Fairy-wren, New Holland Honeyeater, Yellow-tailed Black-Cockatoo and the Rainbow Lorikeet.

 Nature is not something ‘out there,’ it is in fact, at our doorstep.

 We are not alone in our cities, and that is a wonderful thing.

name: Damun Equine

 Shadows of turpentine flowers blow across the work – remembering the old turpentine forest.

name: Characters of Newtown
source_excerpt:
This artwork celebrates Newtown’s gritty past – drawing on history, local stories and old photographs while acknowledging the Gadigal and Wangal peoples of the Sydney Basin, who are the traditional custodians of the lands in which this artwork is situated.
 Left to right we have; a bunyip - an ancient Dreaming creature; native flowers; fig of the Port Jackson fig tree, ‘Damun’ – after which this ward has been named. A coffee cup – common in the old days and prevalent now; a boxer – referring to the roughness known in Newtown from 1900 -1980. Stars and rockets - a shout out to the murals opposite; a yellow character - referencing the bees in the area which keep all the plants happy and healthy; a native banksia; a horse and cart – a reference to early forms of transport, a platypus; a water bird; a kangaroo; a characterised bird in old style attire; the red wattle flower; a new style tattoo - showing the changes in traditional street style as well as graffiti; an apple – representing the fruiting of the area; a Pug - showing the area’s love for dogs and dog friendly venues.

name: The Portal
source_excerpt:
The old wall opens to an imaginary portal, inviting the viewer to discover the story inside. The plants hanging to the sides frame the picture. In the foreground are two large, well-known monumental structures of Balmain, the Post Office, the Courthouse and Town Hall. A tram passes by, a nod to the popular commuter which transported people for many years, carrying the number 2041, the Balmain postcode. 
 A workman in blue walks down the street, a nod to the iconic mural that once featured on the wall of the original Balmain Mechanical Repairs workshop on Darling Street. 
 Left is Arthur Stace, better known as Mr. Eternity, who may have once strolled the streets of Balmain. In his teens his family had a house close by at 5 Moore Lane, Rozelle. Inscribing ‘Eternity’ in white or yellow chalk on the footpaths he travelled, he remains immortalized in the memory of residents and the history of Sydney. 
 
 To the right, we observe people in the company of others, enjoying a snack or drink at Forli restaurant. 
 
 A couple of girls (modelled on the artists daughters) run happily, leaving the past behind and looking towards the future. At the same time, birds fly across the sky, from inside the picture portal to outside.

name: We Run as One

This street artwork depicts local legend Arran Keith, 14, as he enjoys the famous Bay Run with his friends and community. 
 He says, “able bodied or with a disability, we run together as one.” Arran is a record holding frame runner and advocate for disability inclusion in sports. Frame running is designed for people with impaired balance who are not able to run unassisted. 
 Arran says, “I am very lucky to live in a great and supportive community who accept me for who I am and I cannot thank Rozelle & Running Science enough for all they have done. As a person living with a disability like cerebral palsy, being and actually feeling included in your local community is what’s important! I think this mural captures that feeling, that spirit, that moment."

name: Unfolding Memories
source_excerpt:
Growing up in Annandale, I find profound inspiration in the intersection of personal memories intertwining with the area’s transformation over time. 
 
 Immersed in a tapestry of memories, experiences, and connections, the Abby, the Light rail and archways, the horse trots, the greyhounds and the abundant community of dogs on the streets, coffee shops at every corner and constant flow of pedestrians. Every motif portrays the essence of a neighbourhood teeming with life, potential, resilience, and stories waiting to be told. 
 
 As the brush finally settles, I hope the artwork stands as a testament to the resilience of this community, forever embracing the nostalgia of the past while welcoming the winds of change that continue to shape Annandale’s destiny through every resident and the next generations to come. - Smackas

name: Memory Lane
source_excerpt:
The terrace house facade is transformed into an imaginary art gallery in homage to the history of Annandale. 
 
 Using the trompe l’oeil technique, the gallery wall features three gold gilt framed sepia images of archival photographs of early Annandale, including the pair of witches houses, Johnston Street 1880, and the imposing heritage-listed aqueduct, a concrete engineering feat, and marvel of its day. A fourth frames the old map of Annandale Farm from which the area formed and is named (we can only see the top of this frame and map).
 
 In the centre, a fifth colour painting represents a modern-day scene of neighbourhood kids playing on the aqueduct. Archie, Lulu, and Alfie climb the Aqueduct, while local resident Eloise pushes Wren on his trike and Renzo rides ahead on his on bike. The local neighbourhood dog Winnie gazes out. 
 
 The Annandale aqueduct is still fully functioning, and can be seen extending over White’s Creek, just across the road.
 
 The artist wishes to acknowledge the traditional owners of the land, the Gadigal people. Sadly, there are no photographs of Annandale prior to clearing and settlement, as the camera had not yet been invented.

name: Fishers Reserve Waterhole
source_excerpt:
This artwork is a vivid tribute to the Petersham Waterhole, once found in the place of Fishers Reserve Road. It reflects the native fauna which would have been found around billabongs, waterholes and waterways across traditional Aboriginal Lands of the Sydney Basin.
 Zachary Bennett-Brook’s bright and vibrant water patterns flow across the wall, reflecting the once watery environment. Intertwined with the detailed brushwork is Alex Bebbington’s water moths and dragonfly revealing the beauty of the local insect inhabitants and the story of a rich cultural past.
 In the artwork, to the left you see the Mistletoe Moth (Comocrus behri), a day flying moth, feeding on native mistletoe found throughout mainland Australia. Top right, the White Stemmed Acacia Moth (Chelepteryx chaleptyrx) is depicted, one of the largest moths found throughout Sydney, feeding on native Acacia. Bottom right, is the Adams Emerald Dragonfly (Archaeophya adamsi), found in select areas of eastern Australia, it is one of Australia’s rarest dragonflies with only a few specimens ever collected.

name: Tributary
source_excerpt:
Situated in a place where rainfall starts its journey south to Goolay’yari (Cooks River), Tributary speaks to the natural world reliant on these waters. A small stream appears on the corner of Dickson Street in heavy rains, and historical documentation notes the presence of an intermittent waterway here. The water feeds into the drains and canals where wetlands and waterholes once sat, making its way through the now largely urbanised and concreted Gumbramorra wetlands, and into Goolay’yari (Cooks River). Tributary explores water cycles and the interrelation of ecology with urbanisation, making the invisible visible. Under the watchful eye of the largest of the local Kingfishers, a Kookaburra, the hilly country of Newtown and Enmore, feeds water through Marrickville and Sydenham, into the river, the Kamay (bay) and Sea. Black Wattle, Gumtrees, Paperbarks, Native Raspberry and Gymea Lillies flourish, while a piercing orange sunset frames the scene. 
 Telegraph poles and vapour streams from the nearby airport are a subtle reference to contemporary Newtown. 
 
 David Cragg is an artist of Irish, Scottish, Bundjalung and Biripi ancestry, working in Dharawal Country, but who grew up on local Wangal, Gadigal and Bidjigal Country. 
 David sees this artwork as a way of giving back to the lands that raised him and the vibrant communities that call the area home.

We love Enmore. It accepts everyone no matter who they are, who they love or where they come from. The area is full of diversity, people of all ages, ethnicities, and persuasions come here and have fun, enjoy what the area has to offer, but most of all, everyone is accepted for their individuality. - a local resident.

name: We Reap What You Sow
source_excerpt:
Shadow Whisperers are the backbone of Aboriginal existence.
 These spirits have been passing down knowledge for hundreds of thousands of years. The stories they share are about the fragility of land and life and how we need to care for and respect all these things, in stark contrast to our reality.
 The Shadow Whisperers tell stories of life and death cycles. They remind us that whatever energy we take from the earth, we must replace – with song, dance, art, time, messages, love, care and action.
 These beings are drawn as shadows of ourselves, honouring our old people and stories that have been silenced. For all living things that don’t have a voice. They show us messages through climate catastrophes – the language of the land.
 The spirit voices are now guiding us, lifting us up. They have paved the way for us to continue practicing culture and teaching truths and to continue our belief that Sovereignty/Treaty as Aboriginal people is the only solution. - Madwings

name: SOS – Save Our Sons
source_excerpt:
Addison Road Community Centre sits on the edge of the Gumbramorra Swamp area. It was and always will be Aboriginal Land.
 Firstly a military camp and then becoming army barracks in 1916, it was a place for recruiting and training troops for both WW1 and WW2.
 In 1964 Australia introduced national service for young men turning 20, sending them to battle in Vietnam.
 A group of Sydney housewives issued a national “distress call - SOS - to mothers everywhere.” 
 On the Addison Road footpath the Save Our Sons movement was born. 
 The first recruits arriving in June 1965 were met with a large crowd, traffic congestion, TV cameras, SOS protestors, police and Australian Security Intelligence Organisation (ASIO) officers.
 The fervent nation-wide protests and silent vigils lasted another 8 years.

name: Wetland
source_excerpt:
The Gumbramorra wetlands were once a huge multi-pond wetland system, which fed into Goolay’yari (Cooks River). 
 An often impassable semi-aquatic cornucopia of life, now largely hidden underneath the suburbs of Marrickville, Sydenham and Enmore in the form of concrete canals and holding basins. 
 This artwork celebrates the ebb and flow of the water, essential to all aspects of life, for both people and country, living, healing and growing, while also referencing the fragile fertility of the soils, clays, rocks and ochres emerging from the strata of the Gadigal, Bidjigal and Wangal lands that these waters flow through.
 Native to the wetland ecosystem were Gymea Lillies, Lily Pillies, Flannel Flowers, Pea Flowers, Warragal Greens and Ferns, which all feature across the mural, along with a Double-Barred Finch and 
 Willy Wagtail. 
 The flora and fauna featured draws attention to the unspoken language of our precious communion with nature, and the importance of protecting country. 
 David Cragg is an artist of Irish, Scottish, Bundjalung and Biripi ancestry, working in Dharawal Country, but who grew up on local Wangal, Gadigal and Bidjigal Country. 
 David sees this artwork as a way of giving back to the lands that raised him and the vibrant communities that call the area home.

name: Ngurra, We Camp
source_excerpt:
This artwork is inspired by walks along the Balmain East peninsula and its beautiful coastline. In the painting, two images share the same skyline. Right, is a large Baludarri (leather jacket fish) after which the Balmain Ward is also named. Left, is a curious dingo looking into indigenous fish traps establishing a connection with the dingo’s love of fish and also, celebrating the dingo as the original dog of the Sydney basin and also because The East Village Hotel is a dog friendly place. In the sky, left of the Leather Jacket Fish the indigenous constellation of the Dingo Puppies is depicted.
 The fish traps depicted in the painting have been inspired by the beautiful Fish Trap sculptures of Chris Edwards-Clarke, located in King George Park, Manning Street, Rozelle.
 ‘For Aboriginal Torres Strait Islander peoples, ﬁshing is as natural and as necessary as breathing. It forms part of the deep cultural and spiritual connection many communities have with their waters and marine resources, whether saltwater or freshwater. Fishing is a cultural practice and is informed by traditional knowledge. 
 Across Australia, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander ﬁshers are taking steps to ensure their voices and values are heard in ﬁsheries management planning, negotiating catch allowances and controlled access to their waters and marine resources.’ -Chris Edwards
 ‘I want to acknowledge a shared fishing history of the peninsula, the indigenous history, as well as honour the beauty of Sydney Harbour.’ -Elbows
 Both Elbows and Chris Edwards have collaborated to paint this artwork.
 Celebrating art in public places - commissioned by Inner West Council through Perfect Match, matching artists with community to collaboratively produce site specific artworks.

name: Whispers of the Bush
source_excerpt:
This artwork celebrates the Inner West’s local flora and fauna. At the centre is the Christmas beetle, once abundantly found around the Christmas summer, now a rare sight. The Christmas beetle is surrounded by a woodland of Eucalyptus from which it feeds. The visual story tells of the lifecycle of the beetle, from larvae that feeds on the tree leaves, to becoming a mature beetle. 
 A Dragonfly flies over a pool of water, we included this to pay tribute to the nearby Cooks River.
 We want the viewers to be immersed in the life of those beautiful creatures, and feel right ‘inside the bush,’ We hope this brings awareness about these beautiful creatures and of how we can help support our local Christmas beetles and dragonflies by planting and looking after our Eucalyptus trees and taking care of our local rivers.

name: Stanmore House
source_excerpt: Stanmore House is of State heritage significance for its associations with Mary Reibey a noted emancipist entrepreneur and the Long Innes family. Constructed circa 1847-1855 by Mary Reibey for her daughter Elizabeth Anne and son-in-law, Captain Joseph Long Innes.  It is claimed that Innes' son Sir Joseph Long Innes, later Attorney General of New South Wales was born in Stanmore house in 1834.  Stanmore House is a rare surviving architectural example of its period and has a unique ability to demonstrate a way of life when Newtown was considered a fashionable suburb.  It is the last of the large suburban villas remaining in Newtown/Enmore from the period preceding the railway line, after which the suburb changed dramatically.  The house has the ability to demonstrate the conscious attempts of the rich merchant class to recreate the marriage of architecture with landscape of the English Picturesque movement.  Stanmore House is the last vestige of that era in Newtown and has unique social value in its ability to demonstrate a way of life. Stanmore House has been attributed to Henry Robertson who was a leading Sydney architect of the first half of the nineteenth century.  It is the only known surviving house by him.  The internal finishes of Stanmore House are of a high quality, and are largely intact.  (Heritage Office files) (Long 1989)

name: Newtown Railway Station group and Former Newtown Tramway Depot
source_title: Newtown Railway Station group and Former Newtown Tramway Depot
source_excerpt:
Newtown Railway Station is of state significance, representing three significant historical phases in the development of the NSW railways. The original Newtown Station to the west of the existing site was one of only five original intermediate stations on the first railway line in NSW between Sydney and Parramatta Junction. The subsequent two stations built on the existing station site date from the 1891 quadruplication and 1927 sextuplication of the line representing the expansion of the railways in the late 19th and early 20th Century to accommodate increasing rail services. 
      The station is significant in terms of its 1892 overhead booking office which is an important and recognisable element in the streetscape, and is a rare structure being one of only three similar structures in the state representing the earliest use of above-platform buildings. The building along with the King Street overbridge collectively demonstrates a former era of travel. 
      The former Newtown tram depot has state historical significance as it formed an integral part of the electrification of the NSW tramway system which commenced in 1899.  Being the second of the tram depots built to service the new electric tram fleet the buildings, it represents the high level of commitment by the government to providing a mass electric transit system service for Sydney's suburbs at the start of the 20th century.
      The tram depot site and its buildings are representative of the typical electric tram depot layout constructed as part of the NSW tramway system. The large tram shed and the associated tram offices exemplify the common architectural style of the NSW tramway buildings built during and just after the time of Federation.  It is considered rare as it is one of the few NSW tramway buildings to survive and it is the oldest in essentially its original form.

name: St Stephen's Anglican Church and Cemetery
source_title: St Stephen's Anglican Church and Cemetery
source_excerpt: This building is one of Australia's best Gothic Revival churches on this scale and its unique and historic surroundings render it a building of the highest importance.  The church is in a prominent position on the crest of a rise, approximately three miles south west of the city of Sydney.  The spire is notable for miles.  The cemetery forms a unique close to the Church; it contains numerous fine trees including a large Moreton Fig Tree. (Lucas 1975)

name: St Peters Railway Station group
source_excerpt:
This is a good example of a standard early second class building and forms part of a group of structures in the area that indicate the early history of the station.  It also demonstrates adaptibility with the original small 2 bay awning on one face and the later cantilevered awning to the rear or former street facade of the building.  It is the last remnant at the site of the early period of railway development.
      Brick retaining walls are a significant part of the heritage as the railway builders sought to locate lines in restricted space without resuming too much property.

name: Uniting Church and Pipe Organ
source_excerpt:
The Uniting Church, formerly the Wesleyan Chapel has important associations for Australian Wesleyan Methodists in that its origins were determined by the ideas promulgated by Frederick J. Jobson, secretary of the Wesleyan Methodist Conference in 1842.  Out of the deliberations of the conference came the decision to hold a competition for a 'Model Church'  It was the winning design that formed the basis for this building albeit modified by George Mansfield. (Heritage Office files)
      The organ was designed by a renowned firm of organ makers and has been a part of the Church since 1878.  The modification made to it in 1910 were carried out by a prominent Australian firm.  (Heritage Office files)

name: NSW Aboriginal Education Consultative Group Office
source_title: NSW Aboriginal Education Consultative Group Office
source_excerpt:
The Aboriginal Education Consultative Group (AECG) office and Records is of state heritage significance as the office and working core of the peak Aboriginal Education body in NSW. The NSW AECG has historically turned the tide on the exclusion of Aboriginal people from European education and provided the first NSW Aboriginal Education Policy, support materials and actions to be produced and mandated in NSW schools. This policy was in fact the first Aboriginal  Education Policy to be developed in Australia.  
      The state heritage significance of the NSW AECG office and Records in Stanmore is enhanced through its association with the NSW AECG, the community based and democratic organisation that has worked tirelessly to make the Aboriginal community's voice heard loud and strong in the NSW educational system. The state heritage significance of the item also derives from association with numerous important Aboriginal education activists and leading figures in the NSW Aboriginal community.
      The NSW AECG office and Records is of social significance at a state level for its special association with the Aboriginal community across NSW. This is expressed in the structure of the organisation which ensures that local Aboriginal people have a say in the education of their children through local AECGs which in turn report ideas and information through regional AECG and finally to the peak AECG situated at the Cavendish Property. The inclusiveness is expressed through modifications to the building to accommodate meetings of state wide representatives and access to resources for those involved in education all over NSW. Its location away from the education bureaucracy reinforces it independence and community base.
      The NSW AECG office and records is a rare example of a building which is the home of the peak organization concerned with Aboriginal Education in NSW. The combined physical resources, organisation minutes, reports and educational resource documents housed there represents a significant research resource on the history of Aboriginal education in NSW.

name: Imperial Hotel, Erskineville
source_excerpt:
The Imperial Hotel is of State significance as a venue that has encouraged, welcomed and fostered the LGBTQIA+ community in NSW since 1983. Emerging at a time when laws regarding homosexuality in NSW were being amended, the Imperial Hotel with its inclusive policies and regular drag shows provided a safe space for the LGBTQIA+ community in Sydney to meet and mingle away from the Oxford Street precinct. The hotel gained a national and international reputation for its live shows after the release of the 1994 Australian film The Adventures of Priscilla, Queen of the Desert, which was partially filmed at the hotel and featured its drag shows in the opening and closing sequences. Shows based on the film became a regular feature at the hotel afterwards. 
      The Imperial Hotel is also of State aesthetic significance as an iconic LGBTQIA+ landmark that has been woven into the urban fabric of the LGBTQIA+ community of NSW. The significance is  further demonstrated by the hotel's inclusion in the internationally successful Australian film The Adventures of Priscilla, Queen of the Desert. The aesthetic value of the hotel is embodied in the overall appearance of the external facade that remains largely unchanged and distinctly recognisable as an LGBTQIA+ venue connected to an iconic LGBTQIA+ film. 
      The hotel is of State associative significance as it was one of Dawn O'Donnell's many LGBTQIA+ businesses and was instrumental in the development of the Newtown/Erskineville LGBTQIA+ precinct from the 1980s.

name: Former St Peter's Theatre facade
source_excerpt: The façade has historic and aesthetic significance. It was   built as part of the former St Peters Theatre, one of several former theatres in King Street all of which are from different periods of development and all differing in architectural style. It is  a fine example of the  Federation Romanesque style and demonstrates many of the key characteristics of the style. It was   designed by prominent architect Emile Sodersten and is  a dominant element at the southern end of King Street where the commercial buildings diminish at the railway line overpass.

name: Holy Trinity Church of England & Hall
source_title: Holy Trinity Church of England & Hall
source_excerpt:
The Holy Trinity Anglican Church, Erskineville is a fine and very intact example of the work of the Blacket Brothers, sons of the distinguished architect Edmund T Blacket. The site is also historically significant for its association with Erskine Villa, one of the early villas in the area and the church’s first rectory, and with the history of the growth of the Anglican Church in  inner city Sydney. 
      Architecturally the site contains  a highly accomplished Arts and Crafts Church featuring many fine details, such as the open trussed roof, bell turret, detailed brickwork and some original furniture. It is aesthetically rare as one of the last churches to be designed in the Arts and Crafts style  by the Blacket brothers and as a late Victorian  inner city church of relatively modest size.

name: Former Government Savings Bank of NSW
source_title: Former Government Savings Bank of NSW

name: Bank Hotel
source_excerpt: The Bank Hotel is a good example of a  Victorian Hotel with alterations dating from the key period of hotel rebuilding in the Federation and Inter War periods. The Bank Hotel is part of an important  group of hotels on King Street which also includes the Marlborough Hotel, the Newtown Hotel, the Union Hotel and the Town Hall Hotel. The Bank Hotel is significant to the local area primarily for its historic values associated with its long and continuing use as a hotel in a prominent location adjacent to Newtown Bridge. The Bank Hotel has retained the same name over 120 years holding a long association for the people of the local area. Aesthetically the building demonstrates the modification  over time of a late Victorian hotel, and best represents  the Inter War Art Deco style resulting from 1930 alterations to the façade. The hotel contributes to the King Street streetscape through its form scale siting and disparate detailing elements. With the other nearby buildings the Bank Hotel contributes to a significant precinct of buildings around Newtown Bridge.

name: Erskineville Town Hall
source_excerpt:
The Erskineville Town Hall  has historic significance for its ability to demonstrate the growth of small inner city municipal councils from the 1870s to the 1940s and especially the development of the Erskineville Municipal Council.  It is significant to the local community for its associations with people and events prominent in the development of Erskineville. The form, fabric and layout of the building demonstrates the self image and aspirations of local government circa 1938.  
      It has aesthetic significance as a substantially intact  small scale  Inter-war Mediterranean style Town Hall designed by Lindsay Scott which  provides a  civic focus for the Erskineville Road shopping precinct.

name: Former brickworks group
source_excerpt:
The Bedford  Brickworks site is a significant component of one of Sydney's oldest and most important industries. It retains sufficient material, and occupies an appropriate site to present a clear indication of the working of the site. 
      The Brickworks formed a vital component of the labour force of the St Peters district for several generations and contributed largely to the construction of the district itself. 
      The Brickworks, in its Sydney Park setting, reveals the relationship between several types of industrial activity and between the structure and urban open space.
      The entire site constitutes a landmark that contributes to the stark industrial character of the streetscape. 
      Significant views and vistas that contribute to enhance the significance of the site include the  views and vistas along the Princes Highway; along Sydney Park Road; to the site from Sydney Park hills; and from Sydney Park Road to the city to the north and to Sydney Airport to the south.

name: Erskineville Hotel
source_excerpt: The unusual and striking design of the Erskineville Hotel  by  prominent architects Copeman, Lemont & Keesing makes a strong visual impression.  Its clear aesthetic appeal makes a strong contribution to the streetscape, reinforced by its open and prominent corner position.  The external aspect of the Erskineville Hotel at the first floor and parapet levels appears significant as a highly intact and rare example of a resolved Art Deco design.  However, alterations to the ground floor detract from its streetscape contribution, an impression reinforced by the profusion of signage and advertising at this level.

name: Union Hotel
source_excerpt: The Union Hotel is a good example of an Inter-War Functionalist style hotel, which dates from the key period of Hotel rebuilding by the major breweries in NSW.  The Union Hotel is part of an important group of Inter -war Hotels located on King Street, which also includes the Marlborough Hotel and the Town Hall Hotel.  The building was designed by prominent hotel architects, Rudder and Grout, who were responsible for many hotels in NSW during the 1920s and 1930s.

name: Newtown Post Office
source_excerpt:
The  former Newtown Post Office   has local  historic and aesthetic significance. The site was the location of a Post Office  from the  1850s  until  2013. The construction of the extant building in 1893, dates from the key period of development for King Street and Newtown as a direct result of the  subdivision,   growth of  the area and the development of King Street as a major commercial  strip during the late 19th century.  
      The building  is a  fine example of  the  Federation Anglo-Dutch style  applied  in an inner city context which, with its tall clock tower,  is a prominent element within the streetscape.   It was one of the earliest buildings in the career of NSW Government Architect Walter Liberty Vernon, and marks a change from the classical style of architecture of his predecessor, James Barnet.

name: Former Globe Worsted Mills, including interiors
source_title: Former Globe Worsted Mills, including interiors

Former Globe Worsted Mills, including interiors and former Globe Worsted Mills substation.
      A major industrial streetscape illustrating the rapid development of local woollen mills in the post war years.

name: Stead House (circa 1850s, also known as Frankfort Villa and Waterloo Villa), including interiors
source_title: Stead House (circa 1850s, also known as Frankfort Villa and Waterloo Villa), including interiors
source_excerpt:
Stead House (circa 1850s, also known as Frankfort Villa and Waterloo Villa), including interiors.
      Stead House is one of the earliest residences remaining in the Municipality. Its conversion to a hospital in 1911 is typical of the changing use of the early villa estates in the early part of the 20th century.

name: Josiah Gentles Victorian italianate style villaThe Towers, including interiors
source_title: Josiah Gentles Victorian italianate style villaThe Towers, including interiors
source_excerpt:
Moorebank, aka The Towers, is of historical significance for its strong historical  association with Josiah Gentle and his family,  as the residence of Josiah Gentle, brickmaker, founder of the Bedford Brickworks, and his family. 
      The house was built for Gentle in 1896 following the subdivision and demolition of Holmwood. 
      Gentle was a successful and prominent brickmaker, a major local employer, and also the developer of other properties in the area.
      The house  is  of aesthetic significance as a very fine Victorian Italianate/Victorian Filigree style house featuring elaborate and unusual features and detailing, most particularly the 3-storey tower, elaborate leadlight front door, sidelights and fanlights, and cast iron classical goddess motifs incorporated into the cast iron balcony balustrading (likely  representing Nike, Greek goddess of victory and triumph).
      Rare for its distinctive and elaborate detailing. The house is also of aesthetic significance for its contribution to the streetscape, and visual association with Nos. 17-23 Dickson Street, a row of elaborate Victorian Filigree style terraces also built by Josiah Gentle.
      A fine representative example of a Victorian Itallianate/Victorian Filigree style building with distinctive features and considered rare for its elaborate detailing.

name: St Joseph's Roman Catholic Church, including interiors
source_title: St Joseph's Roman Catholic Church, including interiors
source_excerpt: This church is associated with the village settlement along the Parramatta Railway Line which was opened in 1854. It is a large building on a prominent site and the rapid growth of its associated schools illustrates the suburban development in the latter part of the 19th century.

name: St Luke's Church of England, including interiors
source_title: St Luke's Church of England, including interiors
source_excerpt: This site forms an important visual link between the Enmore Road Retail Precinct and the fine row of the late Victorian and Edwardian houses which lies along the Stanmore Road boundary of the South Kingston Residential Precinct. Its erection in the early 1880's is a reflection of the increasing suburban development in this area at that time.

name: Newington Manor - Victorian gothic villa, including interiors
source_title: Newington Manor - Victorian gothic villa, including interiors
source_excerpt:
This house, set on a large block behind a tall brick and palisade fence, is an excellent example of the large villa residences built on these slopes in the 1870's and 80's. 
      Other good examples from this period remain in nearby streets within a mixed setting of smaller, Victorian and Edwardian houses.

name: Enmore Theatre, including interiors
source_excerpt: By the 1920's Newtown had eight theatres, and strong support for local theatres and cinemas continued until after the Second World War. However, few of these are still being used for their original purpose. This building illustrates the development of suburban theatres in the late 1930's - early 1940's and is of social significance for the local community.

name: Hughenden terrace, including interiors
source_excerpt: A fine example of a large Victorian terrace which illustrates the high social standing of this subdivision in the 1880's. The subsequent change of use to boarding houses, and the more recent trend towards restoration as family homes, reflects the changing status of the area over the last 100 years.

name: Sly Fox Hotel, including interiors
source_excerpt: The Sly Fox (formerly Enmore) Hotel is of historical significance due to the use of the site for a hotel since 1878 and the current 1912 hotel building. The Sly Fox Hotel is of aesthetic significance for its Federation Free style architecture. The Sly Fox Hotel is of social significance for its role as a place of recreation for local hotel patrons in the current building since 1913. The Federation Free style of the hotel is relatively rare in the local area.

name: Camdenville Public School, including interiors
source_excerpt: The school forms part of a small precinct which illustrates the development of public and private schools in the district in the period around the turn of the century. It also illustrates the rapid establishment and development of schools following the introduction of Public Instruction Act of 1880.

name: Cragos Flour Mills site, including interiors
source_title: Cragos Flour Mills site, including interiors
source_excerpt:
A fine example of a large city mill, built during a period of rationalisation of the milling industry. Its location in close proximity to the city and major transport arteries, with rail access and a private siding, reflects the economic forces affecting the industry at the time of its construction. 
      The whole Crago Mill site is significant as it represents the late nineteenth and early twentieth century phase in milling, characterised by the establishment of large city mills, positioned to gain ready access to the growing export market and the potential for increased profits. 
      The railway siding, the unloading bay for bagged wheat, the timber bins, concrete silos and associated elevators, plus the painted signage on the façade fronting the railway, all demonstrate the evolution of wheat handling methods and, most significantly, the 1920's/30's revolutionary change from bagged tobulk grain handling. 
      The conveyance equipment is typical of that used by flour mills in the twentieth century and is representative of goods handling conveyors generally. Its survival in situ from the 1930's is less common and is considered significant for its ability to demonstrate the contextual operation of the silos. 
      The cribbed timber bins are fine examples of a redundant but once common method of grain storage and the closely spaced support posts illustrate the load bearing requirements associated with the support structure. 
      The silo and mill occupy the former railway reserve for the first Newtown Railway Station, built on Sydney's first railway line. The site may have archeological potential to revealinformation about the early railway occupation.

name: Newtown Town Hall, including interiors
source_excerpt:
This is an important building, central to  the old Municipality of Newtown which operated from 1861 - 1948. The building has had a long and varied use as a public facility. The building has landmark qualities due to its siting at this important intersection and is valued as a community resource .
      Newtown Town Hall provides a physical record of the nineteenth century geography of Newtown. Its retention for alternate uses provides a physical evidence of the history of the area.
      The former town hall continues to occupy a commanding position in the streetscape.
      It has been assessed as belonging to a state-significant group of civic buildings which also includes the former ANZ Bank, the former National Australia Bank, the Newtown Court  House and former Police Station.

name: Vic on the Park Hotel, including interiors
source_title: Vic on the Park Hotel, including interiors
source_excerpt: The Vic on the Park Hotel has cultural heritage significance for historical, aesthetic and representative values at a local level as an early hotel site in Marrickville in operation since 1878. The hotel is one of the only hotels to be built in Marrickville during the suburb’s rapid residential development in the late nineteenth century that still remains in operation. It has significance for its ability to demonstrate the growth of the suburb. The hotel was substantially renovated in c1925 by Tooth & Co and demonstrates the historical process of hotel renewal undertaken by large breweries in the early twentieth century. Despite later modifications, the hotel is largely intact and has aesthetic and representative values as a fine example of an interwar Free Classical hotel created during this process of renewal, with landmark qualities in its streetscape. This pub is likely to have some social significance to the local community.
